claim: The S-phase checkpoint in budding yeast results in the slowing of replication by Rad53-dependent inhibition of the initiation factors Sld3 and Dbf4.
source: The S-phase checkpoint for example results in the slowing of replication, which in budding yeast occurs by Rad53-dependent inhibition of the initiation factors Sld3 and Dbf4.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Rad53 phosphorylates Sld3 and Dbf4 throughout the cell cycle at the same sites as in S-phase.
source: Despite this, we show here that Rad53 phosphorylates both of these substrates throughout the cell cycle at the same sites as in S-phase, suggesting roles for this pathway beyond S-phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Rad53-dependent inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 limits re-replication in G2/M, preventing gene amplification.
source: Indeed, we show that Rad53-dependent inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 limits re-replication in G2/M, preventing gene amplification.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 in G1 prevents premature initiation at all origins at the G1/S transition.
source: In addition, we show that inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 in G1 prevents premature initiation at all origins at the G1/S transition.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Addition of 4-NQO to G1 phase cells results in robust Rad53 activation.
source: Addition of the UV mimetic drug 4-NQO to G1 phase cells resulted in robust Rad53 activation, as determined by the accumulation of the phospho-shifted forms of the kinase (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing Rad53 phosphorylation in Figure 1B,C.

claim: A dramatic increase in lower mobility forms of Sld3 occurs when Rad53 is activated in G1 phase.
source: Importantly, we observed a dramatic increase in lower mobility forms of Sld3 when Rad53 was activated in G1 phase (Figure 1B), which was indeed Rad53 dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by phos-tag gel data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Dbf4 is an APC/C substrate and is partially degraded in alpha factor-arrested cells.
source: For Dbf4, which is an APC/C substrate and partially degraded in alpha factor-arrested cells (Ferreira et al., 2000), we also observed a mobility shift in G1 phase coincident with Rad53 activation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Ferreira et al., 2000.

claim: A mobility shift in Dbf4 occurs in G1 phase coincident with Rad53 activation.
source: For Dbf4, which is an APC/C substrate and partially degraded in alpha factor-arrested cells (Ferreira et al., 2000), we also observed a mobility shift in G1 phase coincident with Rad53 activation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 1C.

claim: A Rad53-dependent mobility shift in Sld3 and Dbf4 is observed in G2/M-arrested cells after DNA damage.
source: Significantly, we observed a Rad53-dependent mobility shift in Sld3 and Dbf4, even in G2/M-arrested cells (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Sld3 and Dbf4 are phosphorylated by other kinases in G2/M, such as by CDK.
source: Sld3 and Dbf4 are phosphorylated by other kinases in G2/M, such as by CDK (Holt et al., 2009), giving rise to additional isoforms of Sld3/Dbf4 proteins even in Rad53 null cells (* Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Holt et al., 2009 and supported by data in Figure 1E,F.

claim: 38 phospho-sites in Sld3 are directly phosphorylated by Rad53 in S-phase.
source: Previously, we have identified the serine and threonine residues in Sld3 and Dbf4 that are directly phosphorylated by Rad53 in S-phase (Zegerman and Diffley, 2010). We mapped 38 such phospho-sites in Sld3 and 19 sites in Dbf4.
evidence: This is stated as previous work by the authors with a citation to Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: 19 phospho-sites in Dbf4 are directly phosphorylated by Rad53 in S-phase.
source: Previously, we have identified the serine and threonine residues in Sld3 and Dbf4 that are directly phosphorylated by Rad53 in S-phase (Zegerman and Diffley, 2010). We mapped 38 such phospho-sites in Sld3 and 19 sites in Dbf4.
evidence: This is stated as previous work by the authors with a citation to Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: Mutation of serine/threonine residues to alanine in Sld3 and Dbf4 generates alleles that are refractory to Rad53 phosphorylation in S-phase.
source: Mutation of these serine/threonine residues to alanine in Sld3- and Dbf4-generated alleles that are refractory to Rad53 phosphorylation in S-phase (Zegerman and Diffley, 2010) and are hereafter referred to as sld3-A and dbf4-19A, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as previous work with a citation to Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: The Sld3-A protein demonstrates a dramatic loss of Rad53 phosphorylation in G1 phase.
source: In G1 phase, the Sld3-A protein demonstrated a dramatic loss of Rad53 phosphorylation (Figure 2A), consistent with direct phosphorylation of Sld3 by Rad53 at the same sites as in S-phase.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: Dbf4-19A shows greatly reduced phosphorylation during Rad53 activation in G1 phase.
source: We also observed a similar result with the Dbf4-19A protein in G1 phase after Rad53 activation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Both Sld3-A and Dbf4-19A show greatly reduced phosphorylation during Rad53 activation in G2/M phase.
source: As in G1 phase, both Sld3-A and Dbf4-19A showed greatly reduced phosphorylation during Rad53 activation in G2/M phase (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The sld3-A/dbf4-A alleles are synthetically sick with cdc28-as1 in the presence of sub-lethal doses of 1-NM-PP1.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the sld3-A/dbf4-A alleles are synthetically sick with cdc28-as1 in the presence of sub-lethal doses of 1-NM-PP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 by Rad53 is important in cells that have reduced CDK activity.
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 by Rad53 is important in cells that have reduced CDK activity.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the sld3-A/dbf4-A alleles are synthetically sick with cdc28-as1 in the presence of sub-lethal doses of 1-NM-PP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 by Rad53 is important in cells that have reduced CDK activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the synthetic sickness observed in the growth assay.

claim: Over-expression of Cdc6, forcing the nuclear localisation of the Mcm2-7 complex, and mutation of the CDK phosphorylation sites in ORC is sufficient to induce re-replication in G2/M phase.
source: Over-expression of Cdc6, forcing the nuclear localisation of the Mcm2-7 complex (through an Mcm7-2xNLS fusion) and mutation of the CDK phosphorylation sites in ORC is sufficient to induce re-replication in G2/M phase (Finn and Li, 2013; Nguyen et al., 2001) and has been shown to induce Rad53 activation (Archambault et al., 2005; Green and Li, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Finn and Li, 2013 and Nguyen et al., 2001.

claim: Over-expression of licensing mutants that cannot be inhibited by CDK induces Rad53 activation.
source: Over-expression of Cdc6, forcing the nuclear localisation of the Mcm2-7 complex (through an Mcm7-2xNLS fusion) and mutation of the CDK phosphorylation sites in ORC is sufficient to induce re-replication in G2/M phase (Finn and Li, 2013; Nguyen et al., 2001) and has been shown to induce Rad53 activation (Archambault et al., 2005; Green and Li, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Archambault et al., 2005 and Green and Li, 2005.

claim: Conditional over-expression of licensing mutants that cannot be inhibited by CDK combined with sld3-A and dbf4-A leads to an increase in total re-replication in nocodazole arrested cells.
source: Importantly, conditional over-expression of licensing mutants that cannot be inhibited by CDK combined with sld3-A and dbf4-A led to an increase in the total re-replication in nocodazole arrested cells (Figure 3A – compare flow cytometry overlay red vs. black).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3A.

claim: A dramatic increase in DNA copy number largely for Chromosome III is observed in strains that over-express Cdc6 and pre-RC mutants that cannot be inhibited by CDK.
source: While we did not detect any differences between the mitochondrial DNA content of the strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we observed a dramatic increase in DNA copy number largely for Chromosome III in strains that over-express Cdc6 and pre-RC mutants that cannot be inhibited by CDK (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by DNA sequencing and copy number analysis in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Chromosome III is particularly susceptible to re-replication.
source: Previous studies have indeed shown that chromosome III is particularly susceptible to re-replication (Green et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Green et al., 2006.

claim: Greater re-replication of chromosome III is observed when the pre-RC mutants are combined with sld3-A and dbf4-A.
source: While we did not detect any re-replication in the sld3-A/dbf4-A strain alone (data not shown), we observed greater re-replication of chromosome III when the pre-RC mutants were combined with sld3-A and dbf4-A, which cannot be inhibited by Rad53 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by DNA copy number analysis in Figure 3B.

claim: Rad53-dependent inhibition of replication initiation can reduce inappropriate replication in G2 phase when licensing control is compromised.
source: Together with Figure 3A, this suggests that Rad53-dependent inhibition of replication initiation can reduce inappropriate replication in G2 phase when licensing control is compromised.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3A and 3B showing increased re-replication in sld3-A/dbf4-A mutants.

claim: Re-replication generates head-to-tail tandem gene amplifications, a process termed re-replication-induced gene amplification (RRIGA).
source: One of the consequences of re-replication is the generation of head-to-tail tandem gene amplifications, a process termed re-replication-induced gene amplification (RRIGA) (Green et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Green et al., 2010.

claim: Expression of the licensing mutants by the addition of galactose results in a large increase in RRIGA events.
source: In contrast to wild-type yeast or the sld3-A/dbf4-A strain alone, expression of the licensing mutants by the addition of galactose resulted in a large increase in RRIGA events, as expected (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RRIGA assay data in Figure 3D.

claim: RRIGA events are even greater when the mutants that allow licensing in the presence of CDK are combined with the sld3-A/dbf4-A alleles.
source: Importantly, RRIGA events were even greater when the mutants that allow licensing in the presence of CDK were combined with the sld3-A/dbf4-A alleles (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RRIGA assay data in Figure 3D.

claim: The checkpoint kinase Rad53 reduces gene amplification events after re-replication through inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4, even in G2/M-arrested cells.
source: This assay demonstrates that the checkpoint kinase Rad53 indeed reduces gene amplification events after re-replication through inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4, even in G2/M-arrested cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the RRIGA assay data in Figure 3D.

claim: DNA damage in G1 phase delays the G1/S transition, which from humans to yeast, involves the checkpoint kinase-dependent down-regulation and/or inhibition of G1/S cyclin-CDK activity.
source: DNA damage in G1 phase delays the G1/S transition, which from humans to yeast, involves the checkpoint kinase-dependent down-regulation and/or inhibition of G1/S cyclin-CDK activity (Bertoli et al., 2013; Lanz et al., 2019; Shaltiel et al., 2015; Sidorova and Breeden, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple sources.

claim: DNA damage in G1 phase results in the inhibitory checkpoint phosphorylation of two replication initiation factors, Sld3 and Dbf4.
source: Here we have shown that DNA damage in G1 phase also results in the inhibitory checkpoint phosphorylation of two replication initiation factors, Sld3 and Dbf4 (Figures 1 and 2), suggesting that this might be an additional mechanism to prevent premature DNA replication at the G1/S transition (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Addition of 4-NQO to G1-arrested yeast cells and then release into S-phase results in robust Rad53 activation in G1 phase, such that cells enter S-phase with an already active checkpoint.
source: To specifically analyse the consequences of DNA damage in G1 phase, we added 4-NQO to G1-arrested yeast cells and then released cells into S-phase in fresh medium without 4-NQO. Crucially, this approach resulted in robust Rad53 activation in G1 phase, such that cells enter S-phase with an already active checkpoint (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rad53 activation in G1 phase results in the slowing of the G1/S transition as detected by the delay in budding and the delay in DNA synthesis.
source: Rad53 activation in G1 phase resulted in the slowing of the G1/S transition as detected by the delay in budding (a G1 cyclin/CDK-mediated event) and the delay in DNA synthesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by budding index and flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sld3-A dbf4-A alleles cause little difference in S-phase progression after DNA damage in G1 phase, compared to the wild-type strain.
source: Despite this, the sld3-A dbf4-A alleles caused little difference in S-phase progression after DNA damage in G1 phase, compared to the wild-type strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rad53 inhibits CDK activation through phosphorylation of the Swi6 subunit of the transcriptional activator SBF.
source: As Rad53 is known to inhibit CDK activation through phosphorylation of the Swi6 subunit of the transcriptional activator SBF (Sidorova and Breeden, 1997), we wondered whether Rad53-dependent inhibition of both replication initiation factors and G1/S transcription might prevent precocious DNA replication after damage in G1 phase (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Sidorova and Breeden, 1997.

claim: Swi4-t is a truncated form of the SBF transcription factor Swi4 that lacks the C-terminus required for interaction with Swi6 and thus cannot be inhibited by Rad53.
source: To test this, we over-expressed a truncated form of the SBF transcription factor Swi4 (Swi4-t), which lacks the C-terminus required for interaction with Swi6 and thus cannot be inhibited by Rad53 (Sidorova and Breeden, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Sidorova and Breeden, 1997.

claim: Over-expression of Swi4-t results in faster progression through the G1/S transition in the presence of 4-NQO.
source: Over-expression of Swi4-t indeed resulted in faster progression through the G1/S transition in the presence of 4-NQO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) as expected (Sidorova and Breeden, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by budding index data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The combination of expression of Swi4-t together with sld3-A dbf4-A results in much faster S-phase progression after DNA damage in G1 phase compared to Swi4-t expression alone.
source: Importantly, the combination of expression of Swi4-t together with sld3-A dbf4-A resulted in much faster S-phase progression after DNA damage in G1 phase compared to Swi4-t expression alone (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: The differences in the onset of DNA replication between swi4-t with and without sld3-A/dbf4-A are not due to differences in the G1/S transition as these strains budded at the same time.
source: These differences in the onset of DNA replication between swi4-t with and without sld3-A/dbf4-A were not due to differences in the G1/S transition as these strains budded at the same time (Figure 4C) and both strains also exhibited similar levels of Rad53 activation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by budding index data in Figure 4C and western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: Rad53 activation in G1 phase prevents precocious DNA replication initiation by inhibiting not only G1/S transcription, but also Sld3 and Dbf4.
source: Together this suggests that Rad53 activation in G1 phase prevents precocious DNA replication initiation by inhibiting not only G1/S transcription, but also Sld3 and Dbf4.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data in Figure 4B-D showing faster S-phase progression when both pathways are disrupted.

claim: Activation of Rad53 during S-phase caused by fork stalling/DNA damage at early replicons results in inhibition of subsequent (late) origin firing, which in yeast is mediated by inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4.
source: Activation of Rad53 during S-phase caused by fork stalling/DNA damage at early replicons results in inhibition of subsequent (late) origin firing, which in yeast is mediated by inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 (Lopez-Mosqueda et al., 2010; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Lopez-Mosqueda et al., 2010 and Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: At the earliest time point (20 min), the swi4-t sld3-A dbf4-A strain shows peaks of replication initiation at the earliest firing origins, even though Rad53 is highly activated.
source: At the earliest time point (20 min), while the swi4-t over-expressing strain alone had barely begun to replicate (Figure 4E, chromosome VII as an example), the swi4-t sld3-A dbf4-A strain showed peaks of replication initiation at the earliest firing origins (e.g., see *, Figure 4E), even though Rad53 is highly activated (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by DNA copy number analysis in Figure 4E and western blot data in Figure 4D.

claim: Much greater firing of early origins is observed in the swi4-t sld3-A dbf4-A strain compared to swi4-t alone throughout the time course.
source: By analysis of initiation at all origins, split into quintiles according to their normal firing time, we observe much greater firing of early origins in the swi4-t sld3-A dbf4-A strain compared to swi4-t alone throughout the time course (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by box plot analysis in Figure 4F and replication profiles in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: An increase in later firing origins is observed in the swi4-t sld3-A dbf4-A strain over time, suggesting that the relative timing of origin firing is not affected.
source: Over time, we also observe an increase in later firing origins in the swi4-t sld3-A dbf4-A strain (arrows Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the relative timing of origin firing is not affected.
evidence: This is supported by box plot analysis in Figure 4F and replication profiles in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of Rad53 and inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 in G1 phase contribute to the mechanism preventing the onset of DNA replication from all origins, not just late firing origins, in the presence of DNA damage.
source: Together this demonstrates that activation of Rad53 and inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 in G1 phase contribute to the mechanism preventing the onset of DNA replication from all origins, not just late firing origins, in the presence of DNA damage (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is concluded from the replication timing analysis in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Loss of function of genes that result in a delay in the G1/S transition, such as CLN2, SWI4, and BCK2, improves the growth of sld3-A/dbf4-A in the presence of phleomycin.
source: Loss of function of genes that result in a delay in the G1/S transition, such as CLN2, SWI4, and BCK2 (Di Como et al., 1995), improved the growth of sld3-A/dbf4-A in the presence of phleomycin (suppressors, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), whereas loss of function of genes that would result in the acceleration of G1/S, such as WHI5 and SIC1 (Bertoli et al., 2013), were synthetic sick with the sld3-A/dbf4-A alleles (enhancers, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citations to Di Como et al., 1995.

claim: Loss of function of genes that would result in the acceleration of G1/S, such as WHI5 and SIC1, are synthetic sick with the sld3-A/dbf4-A alleles.
source: Loss of function of genes that result in a delay in the G1/S transition, such as CLN2, SWI4, and BCK2 (Di Como et al., 1995), improved the growth of sld3-A/dbf4-A in the presence of phleomycin (suppressors, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), whereas loss of function of genes that would result in the acceleration of G1/S, such as WHI5 and SIC1 (Bertoli et al., 2013), were synthetic sick with the sld3-A/dbf4-A alleles (enhancers, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citations to Bertoli et al., 2013.

claim: These genetic interactions are consistent with an important role for Rad53-dependent inhibition of origin firing in preventing precocious replication after DNA damage in G1 phase.
source: These genetic interactions are consistent with an important role for Rad53-dependent inhibition of origin firing in preventing precocious replication after DNA damage in G1 phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The checkpoint-dependent inhibition of origin firing limits further re-replication and gene amplifications in G2 phase when licensing control is compromised.
source: By combining tight cell cycle arrests with the separation-of-function mutants, sld3-A dbf4-A, we show specifically that the checkpoint-dependent inhibition of origin firing limits further re-replication and gene amplifications in G2 phase when licensing control is compromised (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: This pathway is likely to be evolutionarily conserved, as checkpoint activation in S-phase in human cells also appears to limit re-replication through inhibition of Dbf4.
source: This pathway is likely to be evolutionarily conserved, as checkpoint activation in S-phase in human cells also appears to limit re-replication through inhibition of Dbf4 (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculated based on a citation to Lee et al., 2012.

claim: Tandem head-to-tail duplications are a prominent feature of many cancers.
source: As tandem head-to-tail duplications are a prominent feature of many cancers (Menghi et al., 2018), knowledge of the pathways that prevent this form of structural variation may be important for understanding oncogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Menghi et al., 2018.

claim: Knowledge of the pathways that prevent tandem head-to-tail duplications may be important for understanding oncogenesis.
source: As tandem head-to-tail duplications are a prominent feature of many cancers (Menghi et al., 2018), knowledge of the pathways that prevent this form of structural variation may be important for understanding oncogenesis.
evidence: This is speculated based on the connection between re-replication and cancer.

claim: The checkpoint inhibition of all origin firing is a failsafe mechanism that prevents precocious S-phase entry when the G1 checkpoint is compromised.
source: The identification of the checkpoint inhibition of all origin firing as a failsafe mechanism that prevents precocious S-phase entry when the G1 checkpoint is compromised described here (Figure 4) may provide a potential mechanistic rationale for the selective targeting of p53/Rb mutant cancers using Chk1 and ATR inhibitors, which are currently in clinical trials (Bradbury et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Mutations in genes such as Rb and p53 that control the G1/S transition and the G1 checkpoint response, respectively, are amongst the most common mutations in cancers.
source: Mutations in genes such as Rb and p53 that control the G1/S transition and the G1 checkpoint response, respectively, are amongst the most common mutations in cancers (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2001; Massagué, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Malumbres and Barbacid, 2001 and Massagué, 2004.

claim: Defects in the G1/S transition result in increased dependence on the checkpoint kinases for survival.
source: Work from yeast to humans has shown that defects in the G1/S transition results in increased dependence on the checkpoint kinases for survival (Rundle et al., 2017; Sidorova and Breeden, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Rundle et al., 2017 and Sidorova and Breeden, 2002.

claim: The identification of the checkpoint inhibition of all origin firing may provide a potential mechanistic rationale for the selective targeting of p53/Rb mutant cancers using Chk1 and ATR inhibitors.
source: The identification of the checkpoint inhibition of all origin firing as a failsafe mechanism that prevents precocious S-phase entry when the G1 checkpoint is compromised described here (Figure 4) may provide a potential mechanistic rationale for the selective targeting of p53/Rb mutant cancers using Chk1 and ATR inhibitors, which are currently in clinical trials (Bradbury et al., 2020).
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study and a citation to Bradbury et al., 2020.

claim: Chk1 and ATR inhibitors are currently in clinical trials.
source: The identification of the checkpoint inhibition of all origin firing as a failsafe mechanism that prevents precocious S-phase entry when the G1 checkpoint is compromised described here (Figure 4) may provide a potential mechanistic rationale for the selective targeting of p53/Rb mutant cancers using Chk1 and ATR inhibitors, which are currently in clinical trials (Bradbury et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Bradbury et al., 2020.

claim: In eukaryotes, the entire genome is replicated once and only once in every cell division by linking DNA replication control to the cell cycle.
source: It is vitally important that in every cell division, the entire genome is replicated once and only once. In eukaryotes, this is achieved by linking DNA replication control to the cell cycle (Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Siddiqui et al., 2013.

claim: The first step in replication is the formation of the pre-replicative complex (pre-RC) at origins – a process called 'licensing'.
source: The first step in replication is the formation of the pre-replicative complex (pre-RC) at origins – a process called 'licensing'.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Licensing involves the origin recognition complex 1-6 (Orc1-6) and Cdc6-dependent loading of double hexamers of the Mcm2–7 helicase on double-stranded DNA.
source: Licensing involves the origin recognition complex 1-6 (Orc1-6) and Cdc6-dependent loading of double hexamers of the Mcm2–7 helicase on double-stranded DNA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Licensing is restricted to late mitosis/early G1 phase by the activity of the APC/C (anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome), which eliminates licensing inhibitors such as cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) and geminin in this window of the cell cycle.
source: Licensing is restricted to late mitosis/early G1 phase by the activity of the APC/C (anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome), which eliminates licensing inhibitors such as cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) and geminin in this window of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which lacks geminin, CDK inhibits licensing from late G1 phase until mitosis by multiple mechanisms.
source: In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, which lacks geminin, CDK inhibits licensing from late G1 phase until mitosis by multiple mechanisms, including direct phosphorylation of Orc2/Orc6 and nuclear exclusion of the Mcm2–7 complex, and by mediating SCFCDC4-dependent degradation of Cdc6 (Blow and Dutta, 2005; Nguyen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Blow and Dutta, 2005 and Nguyen et al., 2001.

claim: Mcm2–7 double hexamers loaded in late M/early G1 phase are inactive, and replication initiation can only occur after the inactivation of the APC/C at the G1/S transition.
source: Importantly, Mcm2–7 double hexamers loaded in late M/early G1 phase are inactive, and replication initiation can only occur after the inactivation of the APC/C at the G1/S transition.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: APC/C inactivation allows the accumulation of S-phase CDK and Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK) activities.
source: APC/C inactivation allows the accumulation of S-phase CDK and Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK) activities (Labib, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Labib, 2010.

claim: DDK directly phosphorylates the inactive Mcm2–7 double hexamers, generating a binding site for firing factors including Sld3/Sld7 and Cdc45.
source: DDK directly phosphorylates the inactive Mcm2–7 double hexamers, generating a binding site for firing factors including Sld3/Sld7 and Cdc45, while CDK phosphorylates Sld3 and an additional initiation factor Sld2, which via phospho-interactions with Dpb11, results in replisome assembly by poorly understood mechanisms (Riera et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Riera et al., 2017.

claim: CDK phosphorylates Sld3 and an additional initiation factor Sld2, which via phospho-interactions with Dpb11, results in replisome assembly by poorly understood mechanisms.
source: DDK directly phosphorylates the inactive Mcm2–7 double hexamers, generating a binding site for firing factors including Sld3/Sld7 and Cdc45, while CDK phosphorylates Sld3 and an additional initiation factor Sld2, which via phospho-interactions with Dpb11, results in replisome assembly by poorly understood mechanisms (Riera et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Riera et al., 2017.

claim: The duality of function of CDK, both as an inhibitor of licensing and as an activator of the replisome, is critical to ensure once per cell cycle replication.
source: This duality of function of CDK, both as an inhibitor of licensing and as an activator of the replisome, is critical to ensure once per cell cycle replication (Diffley, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Diffley, 2004.

claim: Multiple checkpoints exist to regulate DNA synthesis and genome integrity before (G1 checkpoint), during (S-phase checkpoint), and after S-phase (G2/M checkpoint).
source: In light of the importance of the linkage between DNA replication control and cell cycle progression, multiple checkpoints exist to regulate DNA synthesis and genome integrity before (G1 checkpoint), during (S-phase checkpoint), and after S-phase (G2/M checkpoint, Hartwell and Weinert, 1989; Kastan and Bartek, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Hartwell and Weinert, 1989 and Kastan and Bartek, 2004.

claim: These checkpoints are mediated by the PI3 kinase superfamily checkpoint kinases ATM/ATR (Ataxia telangiectasia mutated/ATM and RAD3-related, called Tel1/Mec1 in budding yeast) and the effector checkpoint kinases Chk1/Chk2 (Chk1/Rad53 in budding yeast).
source: These checkpoints are mediated by the PI3 kinase superfamily checkpoint kinases ATM/ATR (Ataxia telangiectasia mutated/ATM and RAD3-related, called Tel1/Mec1 in budding yeast) and the effector checkpoint kinases Chk1/Chk2 (Chk1/Rad53 in budding yeast).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In G1 phase, DNA damage such as UV photoproducts causes checkpoint-dependent delays in the onset of DNA replication by inhibition of G1/S cyclin–CDK activity.
source: In G1 phase, DNA damage such as UV photoproducts causes checkpoint-dependent delays in the onset of DNA replication by inhibition of G1/S cyclin–CDK activity (Lanz et al., 2019; Shaltiel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Lanz et al., 2019 and Shaltiel et al., 2015.

claim: In humans, the G1–S transition is delayed by ATM-Chk2-mediated stabilisation of p53, resulting in expression of the CDK inhibitor p21, as well as by checkpoint-dependent degradation of cyclin D and the CDK activator Cdc25A.
source: In humans, the G1–S transition is delayed by ATM-Chk2-mediated stabilisation of p53, resulting in expression of the CDK inhibitor p21, as well as by checkpoint-dependent degradation of cyclin D and the CDK activator Cdc25A (Lanz et al., 2019; Shaltiel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Lanz et al., 2019 and Shaltiel et al., 2015.

claim: In budding yeast, the delay in G1–S occurs in part by Rad53-dependent phosphorylation and inhibition of the Swi6 subunit of the transcriptional activator SBF (SCB binding factor) leading to reduced cyclin transcription.
source: In budding yeast, the delay in G1–S occurs in part by Rad53-dependent phosphorylation and inhibition of the Swi6 subunit of the transcriptional activator SBF (SCB binding factor) leading to reduced cyclin transcription (Sidorova and Breeden, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Sidorova and Breeden, 1997.

claim: In S-phase, origin firing in unperturbed cells occurs as a continuum throughout S-phase, with some origins firing in the first half (early origins) or the second half of S-phase (late origins).
source: In S-phase, origin firing in unperturbed cells occurs as a continuum throughout S-phase, with some origins firing in the first half (early origins) or the second half of S-phase (late origins).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: When replication forks emanating from early firing origins stall, activation of the S-phase checkpoint kinase response results in the dramatic slowing of replication rates.
source: When replication forks emanating from early firing origins stall, for example due to DNA lesions, activation of the S-phase checkpoint kinase response results in the dramatic slowing of replication rates (Painter and Young, 1980; Paulovich and Hartwell, 1995), which occurs in large part through inhibition of late firing origins (Yekezare et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Painter and Young, 1980 and Paulovich and Hartwell, 1995.

claim: The dramatic slowing of replication rates in S-phase occurs in large part through inhibition of late firing origins.
source: When replication forks emanating from early firing origins stall, for example due to DNA lesions, activation of the S-phase checkpoint kinase response results in the dramatic slowing of replication rates (Painter and Young, 1980; Paulovich and Hartwell, 1995), which occurs in large part through inhibition of late firing origins (Yekezare et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Yekezare et al., 2013.

claim: Checkpoint activation in S-phase in human cells can prevent origin firing through inhibition of CDK activity, for example by Chk1- and Chk2-mediated degradation of the CDK activator Cdc25A.
source: Similar to G1 phase, checkpoint activation in S-phase in human cells can prevent origin firing through inhibition of CDK activity, for example by Chk1- and Chk2-mediated degradation of the CDK activator Cdc25A (Bartek et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Bartek et al., 2004.

claim: In budding yeast, the checkpoint kinase Rad53 blocks late origin firing, not by inhibition of CDK activity, but by directly inhibiting two replication initiation factors: the DDK subunit Dbf4 and the CDK target Sld3.
source: In budding yeast however, the checkpoint kinase Rad53 blocks late origin firing, not by inhibition of CDK activity, but by directly inhibiting two replication initiation factors: the DDK subunit Dbf4 and the CDK target Sld3 (Lopez-Mosqueda et al., 2010; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Lopez-Mosqueda et al., 2010 and Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: Rad53-dependent phosphorylation of Sld3 inhibits its interactions with various other replication factors including Dpb11.
source: Rad53-dependent phosphorylation of Sld3 inhibits its interactions with various other replication factors including Dpb11 (Lopez-Mosqueda et al., 2010; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010), while recent work has shown that direct interaction between Rad53 and Cdc7-Dbf4 prevents DDK from binding to the Mcm2–7 complex (Abd Wahab and Remus, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Lopez-Mosqueda et al., 2010 and Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: Direct interaction between Rad53 and Cdc7-Dbf4 prevents DDK from binding to the Mcm2–7 complex.
source: Rad53-dependent phosphorylation of Sld3 inhibits its interactions with various other replication factors including Dpb11 (Lopez-Mosqueda et al., 2010; Zegerman and Diffley, 2010), while recent work has shown that direct interaction between Rad53 and Cdc7-Dbf4 prevents DDK from binding to the Mcm2–7 complex (Abd Wahab and Remus, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Abd Wahab and Remus, 2020.

claim: In higher eukaryotes, in addition to inhibition of CDK activity, the checkpoint can also inhibit origin firing through direct targeting of the Sld3 orthologue Treslin and DDK.
source: In higher eukaryotes, in addition to inhibition of CDK activity, the checkpoint can also inhibit origin firing through direct targeting of the Sld3 orthologue Treslin (Boos et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2015) and DDK (Costanzo et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Boos et al., 2011, Guo et al., 2015, Costanzo et al., 2003, and Lee et al., 2012.

claim: Multiple mechanisms exist to ensure the robust inhibition of replication initiation in S-phase by direct targeting of Sld3/Treslin and Dbf4-dependent kinase and by inhibition of CDK activity.
source: Therefore, multiple mechanisms exist to ensure the robust inhibition of replication initiation in S-phase by direct targeting of Sld3/Treslin and Dbf4-dependent kinase and by inhibition of CDK activity (Lanz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Lanz et al., 2019.

claim: One function of robust inhibition of origin firing during S-phase in the presence of DNA lesions is to prevent the exhaustion of essential factors, such as topoisomerase activities, by excessive numbers of replisomes.
source: One function of such robust inhibition of origin firing during S-phase in the presence of DNA lesions is to prevent the exhaustion of essential factors, such as topoisomerase activities, by excessive numbers of replisomes (Morafraile et al., 2019; Toledo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Morafraile et al., 2019 and Toledo et al., 2017.

claim: A key proposed feature of the DNA damage checkpoints is that the response is tailored to the cell cycle phase in which the DNA damage occurred.
source: A key proposed feature of the DNA damage checkpoints is that the response is tailored to the cell cycle phase in which the DNA damage occurred (Shaltiel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Shaltiel et al., 2015.

claim: There is very little evidence to suggest that substrate specificity of the checkpoint kinases changes during the cell cycle.
source: Despite this, there is very little evidence to suggest that substrate specificity of the checkpoint kinases changes during the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: In budding yeast, most forms of DNA damage and replication stress converge on the single effector kinase Rad53.
source: Indeed, in budding yeast, most forms of DNA damage and replication stress converge on the single effector kinase Rad53, but how different checkpoint responses in different cell cycle phases can be mediated by a single kinase is not known.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: How different checkpoint responses in different cell cycle phases can be mediated by a single kinase is not known.
source: Indeed, in budding yeast, most forms of DNA damage and replication stress converge on the single effector kinase Rad53, but how different checkpoint responses in different cell cycle phases can be mediated by a single kinase is not known.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge.

claim: This study redefines the scope of the 'S-phase checkpoint' with implications for understanding checkpoint function in cancers that lack cell cycle controls.
source: This study redefines the scope of the 'S-phase checkpoint' with implications for understanding checkpoint function in cancers that lack cell cycle controls.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: This study overhauls our understanding of the cell cycle phase specificity of the 'S-phase checkpoint' and provides a novel mechanism that restricts replication initiation to a specific window of the cell cycle after DNA damage.
source: This study overhauls our understanding of the cell cycle phase specificity of the 'S-phase checkpoint' and provides a novel mechanism that restricts replication initiation to a specific window of the cell cycle after DNA damage.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: In G1-arrested cells in the absence of 4-NQO or in rad53∆ cells, Sld3 can be seen to migrate as a doublet on phos-tag gels.
source: In line with a previous study (Mattarocci et al., 2014), in G1-arrested cells in the absence of 4-NQO (Figure 1B) or in rad53∆ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), Sld3 can be seen to migrate as a doublet on phos-tag gels.
evidence: This is supported by phos-tag gel data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The Sld3 doublet in G1-arrested cells is caused by DDK phosphorylation of Sld3.
source: This was shown to be caused by DDK phosphorylation of Sld3 (Mattarocci et al., 2014), but does not affect the DNA damage and Rad53-dependent phosphorylation of Sld3 described here (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Mattarocci et al., 2014.

claim: DDK phosphorylation of Sld3 does not affect the DNA damage and Rad53-dependent phosphorylation of Sld3.
source: This was shown to be caused by DDK phosphorylation of Sld3 (Mattarocci et al., 2014), but does not affect the DNA damage and Rad53-dependent phosphorylation of Sld3 described here (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The dbf4-19A mutant is refractory to Rad53 phosphorylation but is also a hypomorph and is not fully functional for replication initiation.
source: The dbf4-19A mutant, although refractory to Rad53 phosphorylation, is also a hypomorph and is not fully functional for replication initiation (Zegerman and Diffley, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: The dbf4-4A allele cannot be inhibited by Rad53 but is fully functional for its role in replication initiation.
source: We previously narrowed down the critical residues that are inhibited by Rad53 to four sites and generated a dbf4-4A allele, which still cannot be inhibited by Rad53, but is fully functional for its role in replication initiation (Zegerman and Diffley, 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Zegerman and Diffley, 2010.

claim: Dbf4-4A is less Rad53-phosphorylated than wild type in G1 cells after DNA damage.
source: In similarity to the 19A allele, Dbf4-4A was less Rad53-phosphorylated than wild type in G1 cells after DNA damage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that it is indeed the critical residues in Dbf4 that are phosphorylated by Rad53 outside of S-phase.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is the critical residues in Dbf4 that are phosphorylated by Rad53 outside of S-phase.
source: In similarity to the 19A allele, Dbf4-4A was less Rad53-phosphorylated than wild type in G1 cells after DNA damage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that it is indeed the critical residues in Dbf4 that are phosphorylated by Rad53 outside of S-phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Dbf4-4A and wild type phosphorylation.

claim: Transient reduction of CDK activity in G2/M phase is sufficient to induce re-replication.
source: DNA replication is tightly restricted to S-phase in large part by the action of CDK, which prevents licensing outside of late M/early G1 phase. As a result, transient reduction of CDK activity in G2/M phase is sufficient to induce re-replication (Dahmann et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Dahmann et al., 1995.

claim: No re-replication is detected in the sld3-A/dbf4-A strain alone.
source: While we did not detect any re-replication in the sld3-A/dbf4-A strain alone (data not shown), we observed greater re-replication of chromosome III when the pre-RC mutants were combined with sld3-A and dbf4-A, which cannot be inhibited by Rad53 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated based on data not shown.

claim: No differences are detected between the mitochondrial DNA content of the strains over-expressing licensing mutants with or without sld3-A/dbf4-A.
source: While we did not detect any differences between the mitochondrial DNA content of the strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we observed a dramatic increase in DNA copy number largely for Chromosome III in strains that over-express Cdc6 and pre-RC mutants that cannot be inhibited by CDK (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial DNA analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The role of the checkpoint differs depending on the cell cycle phase in which re-replication occurs in human cells.
source: This has important implications for understanding the consequences of inappropriate re-replication in human cells, where the role of the checkpoint differs depending on the cell cycle phase in which re-replication occurs (Klotz-Noack et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to Klotz-Noack et al., 2012 and Liu et al., 2007.

claim: Failure to inhibit Sld3 and Dbf4 alone has little effect on the G1/S transition.
source: It is interesting that failure to inhibit Sld3 and Dbf4 alone has little effect on the G1/S transition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), probably because Sld3 (and Sld2) act downstream of CDK activation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sld3 (and Sld2) act downstream of CDK activation.
source: It is interesting that failure to inhibit Sld3 and Dbf4 alone has little effect on the G1/S transition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), probably because Sld3 (and Sld2) act downstream of CDK activation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is used to explain the observation.

claim: Two inter-connected pathways are important for restricting replication after DNA damage in G1: inhibition of G1/S CDK activity and direct inhibition of replication initiation factors.
source: This study therefore provides evidence that two inter-connected pathways are important for restricting replication after DNA damage in G1: inhibition of G1/S CDK activity and direct Inhibition of replication initiation factors.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 may increase the window of time where origin firing and licensing are mutually exclusive, preventing re-replication.
source: This likely increases the time for DNA repair to occur before replication begins and may also serve to increase the window of time where origin firing and licensing are mutually exclusive, preventing re-replication.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study.

claim: Inhibition of Sld3 and Dbf4 likely increases the time for DNA repair to occur before replication begins.
source: This likely increases the time for DNA repair to occur before replication begins and may also serve to increase the window of time where origin firing and licensing are mutually exclusive, preventing re-replication.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study.
